children.label: a
children.prompt: Draw a large triangle $ABC$. Then produce (extend) the side $AB$ to $D$.

answer.short: Sample answer: a triangle $ABC$ with $A$, $B$ and $D$ on a straight line, in that order.
answer.worked: Sample answer shown. Draw three non-collinear points $A$, $B$ and $C$ and join them. Extend $AB$ beyond $B$ to $D$. Use this same drawing for parts b and c.

spec.description: Authored sample student drawing, not a supplied source figure. An equilateral triangle is used so subsequent sample measurements are exact.
spec.mathematics: A, B and D are collinear with B between A and D; ABC is an equilateral triangle.
spec.answerVisibility: Solution only; the student edition retains a blank drawing region.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Measure the three interior angles of the triangle and confirm that their sum is $180^\circ$.

answer.short: Measurements vary. The three interior angles sum to approximately $180^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Measure each interior angle with a protractor and add the measurements. Small differences from $180^\circ$ may result from measurement error.

For the sample drawing:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAC&=60^\circ\\\angle ABC&=60^\circ\\\angle ACB&=60^\circ\\\angle BAC+\angle ABC+\angle ACB&=60^\circ+60^\circ+60^\circ\\\angle BAC+\angle ABC+\angle ACB&=180^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Measure the exterior angle $\angle CBD$ and confirm that it is the sum of $\angle A$ and $\angle C$.

answer.worked:
Measure $\angle CBD$ and compare it with the sum of the measured angles at $A$ and $C$. They should agree within measurement accuracy.

For the sample drawing:
$$\begin{align*}\angle CBD&=120^\circ\\\angle BAC+\angle ACB&=60^\circ+60^\circ\\\angle BAC+\angle ACB&=120^\circ\end{align*}$$
Thus the exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.

content.prompt: Explain your answers to these questions.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Can a triangle have two obtuse angles?

answer.short: No. Two obtuse angles add to more than $180^\circ$.
answer.worked: Each obtuse angle is greater than $90^\circ$, so two would total more than $180^\circ$. This exceeds the angle sum of a triangle.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Can a triangle have two right angles?

answer.short: No. Two right angles total $180^\circ$, leaving no third angle.
answer.worked: $90^\circ+90^\circ=180^\circ$. A triangle must have a positive third interior angle, so it cannot have two right angles.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What is the minimum number of acute angles a triangle can have?

answer.short: 2. At most one interior angle can be right or obtuse.
answer.worked: Two angles that are right or obtuse would total at least $180^\circ$, leaving no positive third angle. Therefore at least two angles are acute. A right-angled triangle shows that two is possible.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Can a triangle have an acute exterior angle?

answer.short: Yes, when the adjacent interior angle is obtuse.
answer.worked: An exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle total $180^\circ$. If the interior angle is obtuse, its supplementary exterior angle is acute; for example, $180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Can a triangle have two acute exterior angles?

answer.short: Yes, at the same obtuse vertex. At different vertices, no.
answer.worked:
The two exterior angles at an obtuse vertex are equal and supplementary to the interior angle, so both are acute. For an interior angle of $120^\circ$, both exterior angles are $60^\circ$.

If the exterior angles are required to be at different vertices, the answer is no: this would require two obtuse interior angles.

teachingContext.methodNote: The triangle angle sum restricts possible interior angles. Page 3 defines exterior angles as supplementary to adjacent interior angles and explicitly shows two equal exterior angles at one vertex.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Parts a–c apply the angle-sum restriction; d–e combine this with supplementary exterior angles. Part e has a material ambiguity because the source explicitly permits two exterior angles at a vertex.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher prints a no because two obtuse angles exceed 180°, b no because two right angles total 180°, c 2, d yes if the interior angle is obtuse, and e no because two obtuse interior angles would be required. Parts a–d agree. Part e assumes different vertices, an assumption missing from the student prompt.
answerEvidence.conflict: Part e permits two acute exterior angles at the same obtuse vertex under the source definition on page 3; the unqualified teacher answer is therefore incomplete.

Use straight angles at $W$ and $A$, then the exterior angle theorem.

spec.mathematics: Angle ZAB=151 degrees; angle CBX=119 degrees; exterior angle YCA=theta.

$\theta=90^\circ$.

Use straight angles at $A$ and $B$, then the exterior angle theorem.

Straight angles at $A$ and $B$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle CAB&=180^\circ-151^\circ\\\angle CAB&=29^\circ\\\angle ABC&=180^\circ-119^\circ\\\angle ABC&=61^\circ\end{align*}$$
Exterior angle of $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=29^\circ+61^\circ\\\theta&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: AFS with internal LS and extension AG. Curved callouts target the narrow angle at F and angle LSA.
spec.mathematics: G,A,L,F collinear; angle LFS=30 degrees; angle FSL=63 degrees; angle LSA=24 degrees; angle ALS=alpha; angle GAS=beta.

answer.short:
$\alpha=93^\circ$, $\beta=117^\circ$.

Apply the exterior angle theorem first to $\triangle FLS$, then to $\triangle ALS$.
answer.worked:
Exterior angle of $\triangle FLS$:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=30^\circ+63^\circ\\\alpha&=93^\circ\end{align*}$$
Exterior angle of $\triangle ALS$:
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=\alpha+24^\circ\\\beta&=93^\circ+24^\circ\\\beta&=117^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Three rays GA, GI and GL below a horizontal line ordered S,A,I,L,N. Callout arrows retain their two distinct angle targets.
spec.mathematics: Angle AGI=30 degrees; angle IGL=20 degrees; exterior angle GLN=115 degrees; angle AIG=alpha; exterior angle SAG=beta.

answer.short:
$\alpha=85^\circ$, $\beta=115^\circ$.

Find the angle at $L$, then apply the exterior angle theorem in the two smaller triangles.
answer.worked:
Straight angle at $L$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle GLI&=180^\circ-115^\circ\\\angle GLI&=65^\circ\end{align*}$$
Exterior angle of $\triangle GIL$:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=65^\circ+20^\circ\\\alpha&=85^\circ\end{align*}$$
Exterior angle of $\triangle AGI$:
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=85^\circ+30^\circ\\\beta&=115^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Triangle HFE, internal GE and HE, and all three extensions. Curved 20-degree callout targets GEH.
spec.mathematics: I,H,G,F collinear; F,E,D collinear; G,E,T collinear; angle IHE=125 degrees; angle TED=32 degrees; angle GEH=20 degrees; angle HGE=alpha; angle HFE=beta.

answer.short:
$\alpha=105^\circ$, $\beta=73^\circ$.

Use exterior angles in $\triangle EGH$ and $\triangle EFG$, with vertically opposite angles at $E$.
answer.worked:
Exterior angle of $\triangle EGH$:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+20^\circ&=125^\circ\\\alpha&=105^\circ\end{align*}$$
Vertically opposite angles at $E$ give $\angle GEF=32^\circ$.

Exterior angle of $\triangle EFG$:

content.prompt: Determine whether each triangle $\triangle ABC$ below is an isosceles triangle. Give reasons.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with A above horizontal BC and both base angles labelled 63 degrees. Ordinary source blue strokes become black.
spec.mathematics: Angle B = angle C = 63 degrees.

answer.worked: $\angle B=\angle C=63^\circ$, so the opposite sides $AC$ and $AB$ are equal. Therefore $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with A above horizontal BC, angle A labelled 55 degrees and angle B labelled 62.5 degrees.
spec.mathematics: Angle A = 55 degrees; angle B = 62.5 degrees.

answer.worked:
Using the angle sum of $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle C&=180^\circ-55^\circ-62.5^\circ\\\angle C&=62.5^\circ\end{align*}$$
$\angle B=\angle C$, so $AC=AB$ and the triangle is isosceles.

spec.description: Right triangle with horizontal BC, vertical CA, right-angle square at C and 40-degree angle at B.
spec.mathematics: Angle B = 40 degrees; angle C = 90 degrees.

answer.worked:
Using the angle sum of $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle A&=180^\circ-90^\circ-40^\circ\\\angle A&=50^\circ\end{align*}$$
All three angles are different, so the triangle is not isosceles.

spec.description: B at left, A above C at right; BA extends beyond A. The 159-degree label lies outside the triangle beside AC; 74 degrees is inside at B.
spec.mathematics: Interior angle B = 74 degrees; exterior angle at A = 159 degrees.

answer.short: No; the interior angles are $21^\circ$, $74^\circ$ and $85^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Using the straight angle at $A$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAC&=180^\circ-159^\circ\\\angle BAC&=21^\circ\end{align*}$$
Using the angle sum of $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle ACB&=180^\circ-21^\circ-74^\circ\\\angle ACB&=85^\circ\end{align*}$$
All three angles are different, so the triangle is not isosceles.

spec.description: A lies upper left, C on a horizontal line and B to its right. BC extends left of C; its exterior angle with CA is labelled 54 degrees. Angle B is 27 degrees.
spec.mathematics: Exterior angle at C = 54 degrees; interior angle B = 27 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: No calculated angles or equality marks appear.

answer.worked:
The exterior angle at $C$ equals the sum of the opposite interior angles:
$$\begin{align*}\angle A+27^\circ&=54^\circ\\\angle A&=54^\circ-27^\circ\\\angle A&=27^\circ\end{align*}$$
$\angle A=\angle B$, so $BC=AC$ and the triangle is isosceles.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with A above horizontal BC, BC extended right beyond C, interior angle B labelled 42.5 degrees and exterior angle C labelled 105 degrees.
spec.mathematics: Angle B = 42.5 degrees; exterior angle at C = 105 degrees.

answer.short: No; the interior angles are $62.5^\circ$, $42.5^\circ$ and $75^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Using the straight angle at $C$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle ACB&=180^\circ-105^\circ\\\angle ACB&=75^\circ\end{align*}$$
Using the angle sum of $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAC&=180^\circ-75^\circ-42.5^\circ\\\angle BAC&=62.5^\circ\end{align*}$$
All three angles are different, so the triangle is not isosceles.

children.prompt: $P$ and $Q$ are points on a circle with centre $O$ such that $\angle POQ=56^\circ$. Calculate the size of $\angle OPQ$.

spec.description: Right triangle PQR with the baseline extended left to M.
spec.mathematics: PQ=x, QR=5, Q=90 degrees, R=45 degrees, P=alpha.
spec.answerVisibility: No calculated angle or equality marks added.

answer.worked:
By the angle sum of $\triangle PQR$,
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=180^\circ-90^\circ-45^\circ\\\alpha&=45^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The angles at $P$ and $R$ are equal, so their opposite sides are equal. Hence $x=PQ=QR=5$.

spec.description: Isosceles triangle pointing right, AM internal, paired 15-degree curved leaders and single equality ticks.
spec.mathematics: AB=AC; BAM=MAC=15 degrees; ACB=alpha; AMC=beta.
spec.answerVisibility: No right-angle marker is supplied at M.

answer.worked:
$AB=AC$, so the base angles at $B$ and $C$ are equal.
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAC&=15^\circ+15^\circ\\\angle BAC&=30^\circ\\\alpha&=(180^\circ-30^\circ)\div2\\\alpha&=75^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Using the angle sum of $\triangle AMC$,
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=180^\circ-15^\circ-75^\circ\\\beta&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Rotated right triangle with right-angle square derived from BA and BC.
spec.mathematics: A=45 degrees, B=90 degrees, C=beta, AB=y, BC=6.

answer.worked:
By the angle sum of $\triangle ABC$,
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=180^\circ-90^\circ-45^\circ\\\beta&=45^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The angles at $A$ and $C$ are equal, so the opposite sides are equal. Hence $y=AB=BC=6$.

spec.description: Obtuse triangle with 30-degree curved leader from below to B.
spec.mathematics: A=120 degrees, B=30 degrees, C=alpha, AB=x, AC=5.

answer.worked:
By the angle sum of $\triangle ABC$,
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=180^\circ-120^\circ-30^\circ\\\alpha&=30^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The angles at $B$ and $C$ are equal, so their opposite sides are equal. Hence $x=AB=AC=5$.

spec.description: Triangle LMN on a baseline extended at both ends.
spec.mathematics: LM=6, LN=x; both base angles alpha; apex gamma; exterior M beta; exterior N 120 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: No additional equality or angle marks.

answer.worked:
At $N$, angles on a straight line give
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=180^\circ-120^\circ\\\alpha&=60^\circ.\end{align*}$$
At $M$, angles on a straight line give
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=180^\circ-60^\circ\\\beta&=120^\circ.\end{align*}$$
By the triangle angle sum,
$$\begin{align*}\gamma&=180^\circ-60^\circ-60^\circ\\\gamma&=60^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Equal base angles have equal opposite sides, so $x=LN=LM=6$.

spec.description: Equilateral triangle with internal apex-to-base segment and separate full-base dimension arrow.
spec.mathematics: All three sides 6; right apex subangle 30 degrees; right base beta; internal base angle alpha.
spec.answerVisibility: No midpoint ticks or right-angle square supplied.

answer.worked:
All three sides are $6$, so the outer triangle is equilateral and $\beta=60^\circ$.
Using the angle sum of the right-hand internal triangle,
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=180^\circ-30^\circ-60^\circ\\\alpha&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Right triangle and internal perpendicular; full hypotenuse dimension 8 is offset from its segment labels x and 4.
spec.mathematics: Outer lower-left angle 90 degrees, lower-right 45 degrees; internal segment perpendicular to hypotenuse; alpha between internal segment and vertical.

answer.worked:
The outer triangle's upper angle is
$$\begin{align*}\text{upper angle}&=180^\circ-90^\circ-45^\circ\\\text{upper angle}&=45^\circ.\end{align*}$$
In the upper internal right triangle,
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=180^\circ-90^\circ-45^\circ\\\alpha&=45^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The hypotenuse segments add to $8$, so
$$\begin{align*}x&=8-4\\x&=4.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Outer right triangle, two internal segments labelled 5, paired external 15-degree leaders and dimension x between their hypotenuse endpoints.
spec.mathematics: Outer left angle 45 degrees; lower-right angle 90 degrees partitioned into 15 degrees, alpha, 15 degrees; internal sides both 5; their opposite interval x.
spec.answerVisibility: No calculated angles or equality ticks added.

answer.short:
$\alpha=60^\circ,\quad x=5$

The internal triangle is equilateral.
answer.worked:
The three angles at the lower-right vertex form a right angle.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=90^\circ-15^\circ-15^\circ\\\alpha&=60^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The two internal sides are both $5$, so their opposite angles are equal. Each is $(180^\circ-60^\circ)\div2=60^\circ$. The internal triangle therefore has three equal angles and three equal sides, giving $x=5$.

spec.description: Rectangle with AC=BC, horizontal CF and five right-angle markers. BC and CF are not collinear.
spec.mathematics: Angle ACF is 165 degrees; alpha is ABC.

answer.worked: Since $AD\parallel CF$, $\angle DAC=180^\circ-165^\circ=15^\circ$ (co-interior angles). Thus $\angle BAC=90^\circ-15^\circ=75^\circ$. Since $AC=BC$, the base angles of $\triangle ABC$ are equal, so $\alpha=75^\circ$.

spec.description: Triangle ABC, M on AC, BM drawn; AM, BM and BC carry double ticks.
spec.mathematics: Angle MBC=36 degrees; beta=BAC.

answer.worked:
Since $BM=BC$, $\triangle BMC$ is isosceles.
$$\begin{align*}\angle BMC&=(180^\circ-36^\circ)/2\\\angle BMC&=72^\circ\\\angle AMB&=180^\circ-72^\circ\\\angle AMB&=108^\circ\end{align*}$$
Since $AM=BM$, the base angles of $\triangle ABM$ are equal.
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=(180^\circ-108^\circ)/2\\\beta&=36^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: CDE collinear; AB, BD, CD, AD and AE have single ticks. Curved leader identifies DAE, not BAD.
spec.mathematics: Angle DAE=20 degrees; alpha is the exterior angle at C.

answer.short:
$\alpha=110^\circ$

Use the equilateral triangle and the two isosceles triangles.
answer.worked:
$AB=BD=AD$, so $\triangle ABD$ is equilateral and $\angle BDA=60^\circ$. Since $AD=AE$, $\triangle ADE$ is isosceles.
$$\begin{align*}\angle ADE&=(180^\circ-20^\circ)/2\\\angle ADE&=80^\circ\\\angle BDC&=180^\circ-60^\circ-80^\circ\\\angle BDC&=40^\circ\end{align*}$$
Since $BD=CD$, $\triangle BCD$ is isosceles.
$$\begin{align*}\angle BCD&=(180^\circ-40^\circ)/2\\\angle BCD&=70^\circ\\\alpha&=180^\circ-70^\circ\\\alpha&=110^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: AD and BC intersect at E; AB=AC=CD. Curved leader targets AEC.
spec.mathematics: ABC=39 degrees, AEC=110 degrees, ADC=beta.

answer.worked:
Since $AB=AC$, $\angle ACB=39^\circ$ (base angles). In $\triangle AEC$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle EAC&=180^\circ-110^\circ-39^\circ\\\angle EAC&=31^\circ\end{align*}$$
Since $A,E,D$ are collinear, $\angle CAD=31^\circ$. Since $AC=CD$, the base angles of $\triangle ACD$ are equal, so $\beta=31^\circ$.

spec.description: Circle centred at O with diameter COB and chords CA, AB; radius OA drawn. Leader identifies ACB.
spec.mathematics: ACB=23 degrees; AOB=alpha and ABO=beta.

answer.worked:
$OA=OC$ (radii), so $\angle OAC=\angle ACO=23^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOC&=180^\circ-23^\circ-23^\circ\\\angle AOC&=134^\circ\\\alpha&=180^\circ-134^\circ\\\alpha&=46^\circ\end{align*}$$
$OA=OB$ (radii), so the base angles of $\triangle AOB$ are equal.
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=(180^\circ-46^\circ)/2\\\beta&=67^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Six-sided outline without a regularity assumption; dashed equilateral ABC, extensions of BA and CA beyond A, and a separate double-tick class AD=DC.
spec.mathematics: ADC=120 degrees; alpha lies between upward BA extension and AD.

answer.short:
$\alpha=90^\circ$

The dashed triangle is equilateral; the outer polygon need not be regular.
answer.worked:
$AB=AC=BC$, so $\angle BAC=60^\circ$. Since $AD=DC$, $\triangle ADC$ is isosceles.
$$\begin{align*}\angle CAD&=(180^\circ-120^\circ)/2\\\angle CAD&=30^\circ\\\angle BAD&=60^\circ+30^\circ\\\angle BAD&=90^\circ\\\alpha&=180^\circ-90^\circ\\\alpha&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Construct angles of $30^\circ$ and $15^\circ$ at point $A$.

answer.short: $30^\circ$ and $15^\circ$ at $A$, with construction arcs retained.
answer.worked:
Construct an equilateral triangle $ABC$ on $AB$: draw arcs of radius $AB$ centred at $A$ and $B$, and join their intersection $C$ to $A$. Then $\angle CAB=60^\circ$.

Bisect $\angle CAB$ using equal-radius arcs from the points where an arc centred at $A$ meets its arms. Join $A$ to the intersection of those arcs to obtain a $30^\circ$ ray. Repeat the angle-bisection construction between that ray and $AB$ to obtain a $15^\circ$ ray.

$$\begin{align*}\tfrac12\times60^\circ&=30^\circ\\\tfrac12\times30^\circ&=15^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Authored sample construction showing the equilateral-triangle ray and its successive bisectors; dashed compass arcs remain visible.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Construct angles of $45^\circ$ and $22\frac12^\circ$ at $A$.

answer.short: $45^\circ$ and $22\frac12^\circ$ at $A$, with construction arcs retained.
answer.worked:
Extend $BA$ beyond $A$. Draw an arc centred at $A$ meeting the extended line at two points equidistant from $A$. From those points draw equal-radius arcs that intersect above the line. Join their intersection to $A$ to construct a right angle.

Use the angle-bisection construction to bisect the right angle, then bisect the angle between the new ray and $AB$.

$$\begin{align*}\tfrac12\times90^\circ&=45^\circ\\\tfrac12\times45^\circ&=22\tfrac12^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Construct an angle of $150^\circ$ at $A$.

answer.short:
$150^\circ$ at $A$.

Construct $30^\circ$ and take its supplement.
answer.worked:
Construct an equilateral triangle on $AB$ and bisect its angle at $A$ to obtain a $30^\circ$ ray. Extend this ray backwards through $A$. The angle between $AB$ and the backward ray is supplementary to $30^\circ$.

$$180^\circ-30^\circ=150^\circ$$

Retain the compass arcs used to construct and bisect the $60^\circ$ angle.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Construct an angle of $135^\circ$ at $A$.

answer.short:
$135^\circ$ at $A$.

Construct $45^\circ$ and take its supplement.
answer.worked:
Extend $BA$ beyond $A$ and construct a perpendicular at $A$ by bisecting the straight angle. Bisect the resulting right angle to obtain a $45^\circ$ ray. Extend this ray backwards through $A$. The angle between $AB$ and the backward ray is supplementary to $45^\circ$.

$$180^\circ-45^\circ=135^\circ$$

Retain the compass arcs used for the perpendicular and the angle bisector.

children.prompt: Tony would like to build some wooden shelves at the end of the recreation room. Each shelf would be an isosceles triangle. Find the internal angles of these shelves.

answer.worked:
The marked corner of each shelf is a right angle. The other two angles are equal because the shelf is an isosceles triangle.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Each remaining angle}&=(180^\circ-90^\circ)\div2\\\text{Each remaining angle}&=45^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Tony would also like to construct a TV table in the shape of an isosceles triangle in the living room. Evaluate the internal angles of the TV table.

answer.short:
$135^\circ$, $22.5^\circ$ and $22.5^\circ$.

Use the shelf’s $45^\circ$ angle and the straight outer wall, then use equal base angles.
answer.worked:
The recreation-room lower boundary and the living-room bottom boundary are parallel because both are perpendicular to the left wall. The straight sloping outer wall therefore makes the same acute angle, $45^\circ$, with each horizontal boundary. The table’s angle at the bottom-right corner is supplementary to this angle.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Table corner angle}&=180^\circ-45^\circ\\\text{Table corner angle}&=135^\circ\\\text{Each remaining angle}&=(180^\circ-135^\circ)\div2\\\text{Each remaining angle}&=22.5^\circ\end{align*}$$
The remaining angles are equal because the table is an isosceles triangle. Its internal angles are $135^\circ$, $22.5^\circ$ and $22.5^\circ$.

Since $XY\parallel BC$, alternate angles give

The adjacent angles on the straight line $XAY$ satisfy
$$\begin{align*}\angle XAB+\alpha+\angle YAC&=180^{\circ},\\\beta+\alpha+\gamma&=180^{\circ},\\\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=180^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
Hence the interior angles of $\triangle ABC$ sum to $180^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle NMX&=180^\circ-90^\circ-20^\circ\\\angle NMX&=70^\circ.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$PQ\parallel AC$, $AP\parallel BQ$ and $BP\parallel CQ$.

Use equal base angles and equal alternate angles.
answer.worked:
$PQ\parallel AC$ is given.
Since $AP=PB$, the base angles of $\triangle APB$ are equal, so $\angle ABP=\angle PAB=\alpha$.
Since $PQ\parallel AC$, alternate angles give $\angle BPQ=\angle ABP=\alpha$.
Since $PB=BQ$, the base angles of $\triangle PBQ$ are equal, so $\angle PQB=\angle BPQ=\alpha$.
The angle sums of $\triangle APB$ and $\triangle PBQ$ give $\angle APB=\angle PBQ=180^\circ-2\alpha$. These equal alternate angles on transversal $PB$ give $AP\parallel BQ$.
Also, $\angle QBC=\angle PQB=\alpha$ (alternate angles, $PQ\parallel AC$). Since $BQ=QC$, $\angle BCQ=\angle QBC=\alpha$, so $\angle BQC=180^\circ-2\alpha$.
Thus $\angle PBQ=\angle BQC$. These equal alternate angles on transversal $BQ$ give $BP\parallel CQ$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Given $BA\parallel GF$, find $\alpha$.

spec.description: Broken line A–B–O–G–F. Preserve the original absence of parallel-arrow marks; the authorised parallel given appears in editable prompt text.
spec.mathematics: Angle ABO is 38 degrees, OGF is 70 degrees and BOG is alpha; the editorial clarification states BA parallel GF.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and alpha are drawn.

answer.short:
$\alpha=108^\circ$.

Draw a line through $O$ parallel to $BA$ and $GF$.
answer.worked:
Draw a line through $O$ parallel to $BA$ and $GF$. The leftward ray splits $\alpha$ into angles of $38^\circ$ and $70^\circ$ by alternate angles.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=38^\circ+70^\circ\\\alpha&=108^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Stepped connector between two horizontal parallel lines. Horizontal lines have double arrows; descending segments have single arrows. Junctions on horizontal lines remain unnamed.
spec.mathematics: Both pairs of marked lines are parallel; 86 degrees is below the upper line to the left of its descending segment, and alpha is above the lower line to the left of its ascending ray.

answer.worked:
Extend the sloping segment through $O$ below $LM$. Using both pairs of parallel lines, the angle below $LM$ and to the left of this extension is $86^\circ$ (corresponding angles). It is adjacent to $\alpha$ on a straight line.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=180^\circ-86^\circ\\\alpha&=94^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Alternating zigzag D–E–N–T–A–L with the two outer segments parallel and matching arrow marks.
spec.mathematics: DEN is 70 degrees, ENT is 120 degrees, NTA is 140 degrees and TAL is alpha; DE parallel AL.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the three given angles and alpha are visible.

answer.short:
$\alpha=90^\circ$.

Use auxiliary lines parallel to $DE$ and $AL$.
answer.worked:
Through $N$ and $T$, draw lines parallel to $DE$. At $N$, the angle between $NE$ and the downward parallel ray is $70^\circ$ (alternate angles), leaving $120^\circ-70^\circ=50^\circ$ between that ray and $NT$. At $T$, the angle between $TN$ and the upward parallel ray is $50^\circ$ (alternate angles). Hence the angle between that upward ray and $TA$ is $140^\circ-50^\circ=90^\circ$. By alternate angles with $AL$,
$$\alpha=90^\circ.$$

spec.description: Two sloping rays meet at Y below two parallel horizontal lines, with all seven source point names and parallel marks.
spec.mathematics: Upper-left angle at N is 70 degrees; upper-right angle at O is 65 degrees; gamma is upper-right at C, beta lower-left at E and alpha at Y.

answer.worked:
The upper-right angle at $E$ is $65^\circ$ (corresponding angles), so $\beta=65^\circ$ (vertically opposite angles). The upper-left angle at $C$ is $70^\circ$ (corresponding angles).
$$\begin{align*}\gamma&=180^\circ-70^\circ\\\gamma&=110^\circ\end{align*}$$
The interior angle at $N$ in $\triangle NYE$ is $70^\circ$ (vertically opposite angles).
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=180^\circ-70^\circ-65^\circ\\\alpha&=45^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Triangle GFH between horizontal parallel lines. GF extends to J; FH extends to I and below H. All source labels and single parallel arrows retained.

answer.worked:
Through $G$, draw a line parallel to $AB$ and $CD$. Its rightward ray splits $\alpha$ into $45^\circ$ (corresponding angles) and $34^\circ$ (alternate angles).

spec.description: Unshaded quadrilateral ETIK, with a right-angle square at K and the three printed angle labels.
spec.mathematics: E is 60 degrees, K is 90 degrees, I is 120 degrees and T is alpha.
spec.answerVisibility: Alpha is not evaluated in the question.

answer.worked:
The interior angles of quadrilateral $ETIK$ sum to $360^\circ$.

spec.description: Quadrilateral QUAD with each indicated side extension, eight point labels and four exterior-angle labels.
spec.mathematics: W,Q,U are collinear; A,U,X are collinear; Q,D,Z are collinear; D,A,Y are collinear. WQD is 86 degrees, QUX is 110 degrees, ZDA is 100 degrees and UAY is alpha.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the three given exterior angles and alpha are shown.

answer.short:
$\alpha=64^\circ$.

Find the adjacent interior angles, then use the quadrilateral angle sum.
answer.worked:
Adjacent angles on each straight line sum to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle DQU&=180^\circ-86^\circ=94^\circ\\\angle QUA&=180^\circ-110^\circ=70^\circ\\\angle QDA&=180^\circ-100^\circ=80^\circ\end{align*}$$
Using the angle sum of quadrilateral $QUAD$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle UAD&=360^\circ-94^\circ-70^\circ-80^\circ\\\angle UAD&=116^\circ\\\alpha&=180^\circ-116^\circ\\\alpha&=64^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Triangle ABC with horizontal BC, apex A, D between B and A, and segment DC. Alpha labels the whole angles ABC and ACB; beta labels ADC. An arc at C spans CA to CB. No equal-side ticks are supplied. The geometry is schematic under the deliberately contradictory assumption.
spec.mathematics: A, D and B are collinear. The stem assumes AB>AC and AD=AC while the two base angles of ABC are both alpha.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and labels appear; derived inequalities and the angle ACD are not supplied.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use angle $\angle ADC$ as an exterior angle of $\triangle BCD$ to show that $\beta>\alpha$.

answer.worked:
The exterior angle of $\triangle BCD$ equals the sum of its opposite interior angles:
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=\alpha+\angle DCB.\end{align*}$$
Since $\angle DCB>0^{\circ}$, $\beta>\alpha$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that $\angle ACD$ is also equal to $\beta$. Now look at the diagram to see that $\beta<\alpha$.

answer.short: $\angle ACD=\angle ADC=\beta$, since $AD=AC$. As $\angle ACD$ is part of $\angle ACB=\alpha$, $\beta<\alpha$.
answer.worked:
Since $AD=AC$, the base angles of isosceles $\triangle ADC$ are equal:
$$\begin{align*}\angle ACD&=\angle ADC\\\angle ACD&=\beta.\end{align*}$$
The ray $CD$ lies inside $\angle ACB$, so $\angle ACD<\angle ACB=\alpha$. Therefore $\beta<\alpha$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Explain how the theorem follows from this contradiction.

answer.short: The inequalities $\beta>\alpha$ and $\beta<\alpha$ cannot both hold. Therefore $AB=AC$.
answer.worked: Parts a and b give $\beta>\alpha$ and $\beta<\alpha$, which is impossible. Thus the assumption that $AB>AC$ is false. Interchanging $B$ and $C$ gives the same contradiction if $AC>AB$. Hence $AB=AC$: the sides opposite the equal angles are equal.

answer.worked: Mark $O$. Set the compasses to a suitable radius and draw a complete circle centred at $O$. Keep this drawing for part b.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Using ruler and compasses only, construct an equilateral triangle $ABC$ in which all three vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on the circle.

answer.short:
An equilateral triangle $ABC$ inscribed in the circle.

Draw radius $OA$ and construct a $30^{\circ}$ angle on each side of $AO$ at $A$. The rays meet the circle again at $B$ and $C$; join $BC$.
answer.worked:
Choose $A$ on the circle and draw $OA$. At $A$, construct a $60^{\circ}$ angle with arm $AO$ on each side of $AO$, using equal-radius compass arcs. Bisect each angle to obtain two rays making $30^{\circ}$ with $AO$. Label their second intersections with the circle $B$ and $C$, and join $AB$, $AC$ and $BC$.

Since $OA=OB$, the base angles of $\triangle AOB$ are equal, so $\angle ABO=30^{\circ}$. Similarly, $\angle ACO=30^{\circ}$. Thus
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAC&=30^{\circ}+30^{\circ}\\\angle BAC&=60^{\circ}.
\end{align*}$$
The remaining angles of $\triangle BOC$ are equal because $OB=OC$. Together with the equal $30^{\circ}$ angles above, this gives $\angle ABC=\angle ACB$. The angle sum of $\triangle ABC$ then gives $\angle ABC=\angle ACB=60^{\circ}$. All three angles are equal, so all three sides are equal.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Prove that $\angle APB$ is a right angle. Do this by drawing the radius $OP$ and working with the angles in the two isosceles triangles $AOP$ and $BOP$.

answer.short:
$\angle APB=90^{\circ}$.

Equal radii give two isosceles triangles. Their exterior angles at $O$ are twice the corresponding angles at $P$ and together form a straight angle.
answer.worked:
Draw $OP$. Since $OA=OP=OB$ are radii, $\triangle AOP$ and $\triangle BOP$ are isosceles. Thus $\angle OAP=\angle APO$ and $\angle OBP=\angle BPO$.

Using exterior angles at $O$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle POB&=\angle OAP+\angle APO\\\angle POB&=2\angle APO\\\angle POA&=\angle OBP+\angle BPO\\\angle POA&=2\angle BPO.\end{align*}$$
Since $A$, $O$ and $B$ lie on a straight line,
$$\begin{align*}\angle APB&=\angle APO+\angle BPO\\\angle APB&=\tfrac12(\angle POB+\angle POA)\\\angle APB&=\tfrac12\times180^{\circ}\\\angle APB&=90^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$

answer.short: Two diameters $AB$ and $PQ$ through $O$, meeting at an angle other than $90^\circ$.
answer.worked: Draw a straight line through $O$, meeting the circle at $A$ and $B$. Draw a different line through $O$, not perpendicular to $AB$, meeting the circle at $P$ and $Q$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Join up the quadrilateral $APBQ$.

answer.short: Join $AP$, $PB$, $BQ$ and $QA$ to form a rectangle.
answer.worked: Use a ruler to join $A$ to $P$, $P$ to $B$, $B$ to $Q$ and $Q$ to $A$, keeping the circle and both diameters visible.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Prove that each angle of $APBQ$ is a right angle.

answer.short:
$\angle APB=\angle PBQ=\angle BQA=\angle QAP=90^\circ$.

Each angle stands on a diameter; equal radii and the triangle angle sum give a right angle.
answer.worked:
Since $OA=OP=OB$, triangles $AOP$ and $BOP$ are isosceles. Let $\angle OAP=\angle APO=x$ and $\angle OBP=\angle BPO=y$. As $A$, $O$ and $B$ are collinear, the angles of triangle $APB$ are $x$, $y$ and $x+y$.
$$\begin{align*}2(x+y)&=180^\circ\\x+y&=90^\circ\\\angle APB&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$
The same argument at $Q$, using diameter $AB$, gives $\angle BQA=90^\circ$. Applying the argument at $A$ and $B$, using diameter $PQ$, gives $\angle QAP=90^\circ$ and $\angle PBQ=90^\circ$. Therefore every angle of $APBQ$ is a right angle.

answer.short: Construct perpendicular diameters $AC$ and $BD$, then join $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ in order.
answer.worked:
Draw a straight line through $O$, meeting the circle at $A$ and $C$. With centres $A$ and $C$ and the same compass opening greater than $AO$, draw intersecting arcs above and below $AC$. Join the two arc intersections. This perpendicular bisector passes through $O$; label its intersections with the circle $B$ and $D$. Join $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ and $DA$, retaining the construction arcs.

The four triangles around $O$ each have two sides equal to the radius and an included right angle, so they are congruent. Consequently the four chords are equal. Each triangle has base angles $45^\circ$, so each angle of $ABCD$ is $90^\circ$. Thus $ABCD$ is a square.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Using a ruler and compasses only, construct an isosceles triangle $ABC$ in which the angle $\angle ACB$ is a right angle.

answer.short:
Construct perpendiculars to $AB$ at $A$ and $B$ on the same side of $AB$. Bisect both right angles; their bisectors meet at $C$.

The base angles are both $45^\circ$, so $AC=BC$ and $\angle ACB=90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Extend $AB$ beyond both endpoints. At each endpoint, mark two equally distant points on the extended line using a compass. From each pair, draw equal-radius intersecting arcs above $AB$ and join the intersection to the endpoint. This constructs perpendiculars at $A$ and $B$ on the same side of $AB$.

Bisect the right angle at each endpoint using the compass angle-bisection construction. Label the intersection of the bisectors $C$ and draw $AC$ and $BC$. Retain the construction arcs.

Both base angles are $45^\circ$, so the opposite sides $AC$ and $BC$ are equal. By the angle sum of a triangle,
$$\begin{align*}\angle ACB&=180^\circ-45^\circ-45^\circ\\\angle ACB&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Thus $ABC$ is an isosceles triangle with a right angle at $C$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Prove that these opposite angles are supplementary. Do this by drawing the radii $OA$, $OB$, $OC$ and $OD$, and working with the angles in the four isosceles triangles they form.

answer.short:
$\angle DAB+\angle BCD=180^\circ$ and $\angle ABC+\angle CDA=180^\circ$.

Equal base angles in the four radius triangles split each opposite-angle sum into the same four angles.
answer.worked:
Draw $OA$, $OB$, $OC$ and $OD$. Each triangle has two equal radii, so its base angles are equal. Let the base angles of $\triangle OAB$, $\triangle OBC$, $\triangle OCD$ and $\triangle ODA$ be $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ and $\theta$, respectively. Then
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAB&=\theta+\alpha\\\angle ABC&=\alpha+\beta\\\angle BCD&=\beta+\gamma\\\angle CDA&=\gamma+\theta.\end{align*}$$
The quadrilateral angle sum gives
$$\begin{align*}2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\theta)&=360^\circ\\\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\theta&=180^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAB+\angle BCD&=\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\theta\\\angle DAB+\angle BCD&=180^\circ\\\angle ABC+\angle CDA&=\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\theta\\\angle ABC+\angle CDA&=180^\circ.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: The inside-centre construction completed with four radii.
spec.mathematics: OAB, OBC, OCD and ODA are isosceles triangles because all radii are equal.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Repeat part b but this time choose points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ so that point $O$ is outside the quadrilateral $ABCD$. Now repeat part c. The proof this time will be a little different, because you will need to take differences as well as sums of angles.

answer.short:
$\angle DAB+\angle BCD=180^\circ$ and $\angle ABC+\angle CDA=180^\circ$ still hold.

Subtract the base angle of the triangle spanning the empty arc when forming the quadrilateral angles at its endpoints.
answer.worked:
Construct a new circle and choose four clockwise points on an arc shorter than a semicircle, as shown. Join the quadrilateral and the four radii. For this labelling, let the base angles of $\triangle OAB$, $\triangle OBC$, $\triangle OCD$ and $\triangle ODA$ be $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ and $\theta$, respectively. Equal radii give equal base angles. Here $\triangle ODA$ spans the empty arc, and
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAB&=\alpha-\theta\\\angle ABC&=\alpha+\beta\\\angle BCD&=\beta+\gamma\\\angle CDA&=\gamma-\theta.\end{align*}$$
Using the quadrilateral angle sum,
$$\begin{align*}2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\theta)&=360^\circ\\\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\theta&=180^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAB+\angle BCD&=\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\theta\\\angle DAB+\angle BCD&=180^\circ\\\angle ABC+\angle CDA&=\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\theta\\\angle ABC+\angle CDA&=180^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The same subtraction argument applies after cyclically relabelling any outside-centre configuration so that $DA$ spans its empty arc.

content.prompt: Prove that a quadrilateral cannot have two reflex angles.

answer.short: Two reflex angles would already sum to more than $360^\circ$, contradicting the quadrilateral angle sum.
answer.worked: Suppose a quadrilateral has two reflex angles. Each exceeds $180^\circ$, so these two angles alone sum to more than $2\times180^\circ=360^\circ$. This contradicts the fact that all four interior angles sum to $360^\circ$. Therefore, a quadrilateral cannot have two reflex angles.

content.prompt: Let $\angle ACB=x$. In the diagram below show that $\angle ABC=90^\circ$.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with an unlabelled point on AC joined to B. Matching double ticks occur on both portions of AC and on the internal segment. Source blue ordinary linework is rendered black under house style.
spec.mathematics: The unlabelled point lies on AC; the three double-ticked segments are equal. A is upper left, B lower left and C lower right. Coordinates provide a representative drawing without supplying numerical measurements.
spec.answerVisibility: Only A, B, C and the three pairs of equality ticks are shown. No x, internal-point label or right-angle marker is supplied.

answer.short:
$\angle ABC=90^\circ$.

The equal base angles in the two isosceles triangles give $\angle ABC=(90^\circ-x)+x$.
answer.worked:
Call the unlabelled point on $AC$ $M$. The marks give $AM=BM=CM$.

Since $BM=CM$, triangle $BMC$ is isosceles, so $\angle MBC=\angle BCM=x$.

Using the angle sum of triangle $BMC$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle BMC&=180^\circ-x-x\\\angle BMC&=180^\circ-2x.\end{align*}$$
Since $A$, $M$ and $C$ are collinear, adjacent angles on a straight line give
$$\begin{align*}\angle AMB&=180^\circ-(180^\circ-2x)\\\angle AMB&=2x.\end{align*}$$
Since $AM=BM$, triangle $AMB$ is isosceles. Its base angles are equal, so
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABM&=\frac{180^\circ-2x}{2}\\\angle ABM&=90^\circ-x.\end{align*}$$
Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABC&=\angle ABM+\angle MBC\\\angle ABC&=(90^\circ-x)+x\\\angle ABC&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Use the exterior angle theorem to prove that $\beta=3\alpha$ in the diagram below.

spec.description: Unlabelled triangle with horizontal base extended rightwards, vertical right side and an internal segment from a point on the sloping side to the lower-right vertex. Three matching double ticks are retained. Ordinary source blue linework becomes house black. Coordinates express the marked equal lengths; no numerical angle or right-angle mark is added.
spec.mathematics: The left-to-intermediate segment, intermediate-to-lower-right segment and right side have equal lengths. Alpha is the left interior angle; beta is the exterior angle between the right side and the rightward base extension. The intermediate point lies on the sloping side.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the source givens and angle symbols appear; vertex names and proof deductions are absent.

answer.short:
$\beta=3\alpha$.

Equal base angles in the two isosceles triangles, followed by the exterior angle theorem, give the result.
answer.worked:
Call the left vertex $A$, the lower-right vertex $B$, the upper-right vertex $C$ and the intermediate point on $AC$ $D$. The markings give $AD=DB=BC$.

Since $AD=DB$, the base angles of $\triangle ADB$ are equal, so $\angle ABD=\alpha$.

Using the exterior angle theorem in $\triangle ADB$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle BDC&=\angle DAB+\angle ABD\\\angle BDC&=\alpha+\alpha\\\angle BDC&=2\alpha.\end{align*}$$
Since $DB=BC$, the base angles of $\triangle DBC$ are equal. Thus $\angle BCD=\angle BDC=2\alpha$.

Using the exterior angle theorem in $\triangle ABC$,
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=\angle BAC+\angle ACB\\\beta&=\alpha+2\alpha\\\beta&=3\alpha.\end{align*}$$

CHAPTER 13
Measurement and Geometry
Triangles and constructions

entries.description:
Geometrical constructions are an enjoyable and practical part of geometry. They have been used for centuries by builders and others professions. Most constructions involve triangles, so we begin with the geometry of triangles.

The study of triangles was undertaken by the Babylonians as early as 3000 BCE. They knew some methods for working out the areas of some triangles. The ancient Egyptians also worked on the measurement of side lengths and areas of triangles.

The ancient Greeks introduced systematic methods for investigating the properties of triangles.

entries.description: 13A ANGLES IN TRIANGLES
entries.presentation: Main topic band; white uppercase text on turquoise.

entries.description:
Proving that the sum of the interior angles is 180°

Doing measurements and experiments on any number of different triangles does not prove a general result – however many triangles you check, there are always more. Here is an argument that establishes the result for any triangle.

The statement of the result is called a theorem. This comes from a Greek word meaning ‘a thing to be gazed upon’ or ‘a thing contemplated by the mind’ – our word ‘theatre’ comes from the same root.
entries.presentation: Bold subsection heading; ‘theorem’ highlighted in pink.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation introducing a theorem and proof; retained as teaching evidence.

entries.description:
Theorem: The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is 180°.

Proof: Let △ABC be a triangle.
Let ∠BAC = α, ∠B = β and ∠C = γ.
We must prove that α + β + γ = 180°.
Draw the line XAY parallel to BC through the vertex A.

Then ∠XAB = β (alternate angles, XY ∥ BC),
and ∠YAC = γ (alternate angles, XY ∥ BC).
Hence, α + β + γ = 180° (straight angle at A).
entries.presentation: Theorem and Proof labels occupy a left column; statements and diagram occupy the right column. Diagram appears between the construction instruction and the alternate-angle deductions.
entries.exclusionReason: Complete supplied proof, not a question or response task; retained as taught-method evidence.

Matching right-pointing arrow marks on XA and BC indicate parallel lines. Interior angles are labelled α at A, β at B and γ at C. All vertex labels X, A, Y, B and C are present.
entries.presentation: Blue linework and parallel marks; dark labels. No numerical angle values or student drawing space.

entries.description:
A shorter notation for angles

In the above proof, we referred to ∠B and ∠C, rather than to ∠ABC and ∠ACB. We can use this shorter notation because there is only one non-reflex angle at each of the vertices B and C. However, there are several angles at the vertex A, so we have to use a longer form, such as ∠BAC and ∠XAB, to show precisely which one we mean.
entries.presentation: Bold subsection heading followed by explanatory prose.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone notation explanation; no practice task.

entries.description:
The exterior angles of a triangle

Let △ABC be a triangle, with the side BC produced to D. (The word ‘produced’ means ‘extended’.) Then the marked angle ∠ACD formed by the side AC and the extension CD is called an exterior angle of the triangle.

The angles ∠A and ∠B are called the opposite interior angles, because they are opposite the exterior angle at C.

entries.description:
Theorem: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the opposite interior angles.
Proof: Let △ABC be a triangle, with the side BC produced to D.
Let ∠A = α and ∠B = β.
We need to prove that ∠ACD = α + β.
Draw the ray CZ through C parallel to BA as shown in the diagram.
Then ∠ZCD = β (corresponding angles, BA ∥ CZ),
and ∠ACZ = α (alternate angles, BA ∥ CZ).
Hence, ∠ACD = α + β (adjacent angles at C).

entries.description:
From this section onwards, you will need compasses for your geometrical constructions. Make sure that your pencil is very sharp.

‘Compasses’ is a plural word. We use ‘a pair of compasses’, just as we wear ‘a pair of trousers’ and use ‘a pair of scissors’. The singular word ‘compass’ is the instrument that navigators use to find magnetic north.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone introductory teaching, retained as reference evidence.

entries.sourceLabel: Using compasses to draw a circle
entries.description:
You are probably used to drawing circles with a pair of compasses, but here is an exercise just to get the language sorted out.

Copy the interval AB and point O on your page. Open your compasses to the length of the interval AB. Then place the point of your compasses firmly into the point O, called the centre. Holding the compasses only by the very top, draw a circle.

This is called drawing a circle with centre O and radius AB. Notice that every point on the circle is the same distance from the centre O, because the distance between the point and the pencil lead never changes.

entries.description:
Draw an interval from any point A on the circle to the centre O. This interval AO is called a radius of the circle. Every radius of the circle has the same length, because the setting of the compasses remained the same while the circle was being drawn.

The word ‘radius’ is used both for the interval AO and for the length of the interval AO. ‘Radius’ is a Latin word meaning ‘a spoke of a wheel’. Its plural is ‘radii’.

entries.description:
Draw a line through the centre O, cutting the circle at A and B. The interval AB is called a diameter of the circle. Every diameter has length twice that of any radius, because a diameter consists of two radii put together.

The word ‘diameter’ is used both for the interval AB and for the length of the interval AB. It comes from Greek and means ‘to measure through’.

entries.description:
Isosceles triangles
An isosceles triangle is a triangle with two (or more) sides equal.
• The equal sides AB and AC of the isosceles triangle ABC to the right are called the legs. They have been marked with double dashes to indicate that they are equal in length.
• The vertex A where the legs meet is called the apex.
• The third side BC is called the base.
• The angles ∠B and ∠C at the base are called base angles.
The word isosceles is a Greek word meaning ‘equal legs’ – iso means ‘equal’, and sceles means ‘leg’.

Constructing an isosceles triangle using a circle
Any two radii AB and AC of the circle opposite are equal. Thus they form the equal legs of the isosceles triangle ABC. The chord BC is the base and the centre A is the apex.
Using two radii of a circle is an easy way to construct an isosceles triangle. It is used in the investigation below.

entries.description:
The two theorems discussed so far are converses of each other. The first (slightly reworded) says:
If two sides of a triangle are equal, then the opposite angles are equal.
The second says:
If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the opposite sides are equal.
These ideas were introduced in Chapter 6.

entries.description:
• An isosceles triangle is a triangle with two (or more) sides equal.
– The equal sides are called the legs.
– The legs meet at the apex.
– The third side is the base.
– The angles opposite the legs are called base angles.
• Two radii of a circle and the chord joining them form an isosceles triangle.
• The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
• Conversely, if two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite those angles are equal.

The word equilateral comes from Latin – equi means ‘equal’ and latus means ‘side’.

entries.description:
The angles of an equilateral triangle are all 60°
Use a protractor to confirm that all three angles of the equilateral triangle that you drew above are 60°.
We can prove this result, provided that we use the earlier result that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
Any two angles in the triangle must be equal because they are opposite equal sides. Therefore all the angles must be equal. Since they add up to 180°, each angle must be 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.

entries.description:
The interior angles of a quadrilateral always add to 360°. Here are two ways to demonstrate this result for a particular quadrilateral:
1 Construct quadrilaterals of different shapes and measure their angles.
2 Cut out a quadrilateral. Tear off the four corners and show that they fit together to form a revolution.
It is much better, however, and a lot less trouble, to give a proper proof.

Theorem: The sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is 360°.
Proof: There are two kinds of quadrilaterals, as shown in the diagrams below. Join a pair of opposite vertices to form two triangles as shown. The angle sum of each triangle is 180°. Hence, the angle sum of the quadrilateral is 360°.

entries.description:
This question provides a proof of the following theorem:
If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the opposite sides are equal.
It uses the method of proof by contradiction, and relies on the theorem that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
If the sides AB and AC are not equal, then one of them is longer. Suppose, for example, that AB is longer than AC. Mark the point D on AB so that AD = AC. Mark the angles in the two triangles as shown in the diagram below.
